docs.title: Is AI demand real?
docs.text: Is the marginal buyer of AI compute real? Nvidia’s Demand Is Real. Its Financing Is Fragile. Bull on demand. Bear on the financing. Nvidia’s orders are real. Price its revenue as financed, not recurring. Demand for Nvidia's chips is real today: Google paid roughly double the market rate for Nvidia capacity while cheaper TPUs were available, a costly revealed preference rather than paper demand. What makes the revenue less secure than the order book implies is how it is financed. Private credit funded the compute platform, a $38 billion Apollo transaction in late May and a $35 billion first tranche from Apollo and Blackstone, so part of the marginal buyer's spending rests on lenders rather than on end customers. Between the ordered chips and working compute sits a power bottleneck, and depreciation schedules may lag obsolescence. The Call therefore prices the revenue as financed, not recurring: once the bottleneck clears, the question is whether end customers keep absorbing capacity at market-rate financing. The demand is structural, not financed: a visibility window that extends a full year across the customer base is harder to manufacture than one customer's beat (the case Invest in Assets makes). Most of the marginal demand is not end-customer demand at all: future revenue is financed through a circular off-balance-sheet arrangement, so the orders overstate what customers will pay (the case Michael Burry makes). The shortage is real and the financing is beside the point: Nvidia ramps production continuously and still cannot follow demand, so recurrence holds as long as supply lags (the case Kris makes).

docs.title: SpaceX: exit or ten-bagger?
docs.text: SpaceX after the IPO: exit liquidity, or the next ten-bagger? SpaceX Is Funding an AI Bet Before the Proof Ahead of the evidence SpaceX’s AI build is credible. The stock has already paid for 10 gigawatts it has not built. SpaceX raised $75 billion on June 12 at a valuation near $1.75 trillion, and the price assumed an AI buildout the meter has not yet recorded: 0.4 gigawatts of compute is deployed against a site plan near 10 gigawatts by the end of 2027. A site-backed plan is meaningful, but it is not cash generation, and the $1.25 billion a month Anthropic pays through May 2029 is contracted demand that still has to prove durable without the capital cycle doing the work. Starlink's $4.4 billion of operating income carries the build, while the widening AI loss leaves shareholders little room for error. The stock therefore moved ahead of the operating evidence: the capacity is credible, and the proof arrives one deployed gigawatt at a time. The price is early, not wrong: at about 100 times trailing revenue SpaceX is no value investment, yet an extreme bull scenario carries it toward $18 trillion over ten to twenty-five years (the case Trey Henninger makes). The 10 gigawatts arrive on schedule and each one earns: over $100 billion of revenue per gigawatt-year against about $12 billion of rental cost, a path to $300 billion of ARR (the case Jeremie Eliahou Ontiveros makes). Lenders have already priced it: they back Starlink's cash and bet the AI spending never drains the company, so the bond market, not the stock, carries the proof (the case JunkBondInvestor makes).

docs.title: Is AI debt 1999, 2008 or neither?
docs.text: The debt behind the machines: 1999 capex, 2008 credit, or neither? The Machines Will Work. The Debt Might Not. Bearish on the credit The machines will earn. The credit stack is where this buildout breaks first. The machines will earn; the question is who carries the paper behind them. Nebius's own terms put compute in backwardation: buyers pay roughly twice as much for six months or less as for one to three years, $40 to 50 million against $20 to 25 million, a signal about duration that a lender cannot ignore. The 95 percent H100 re-let and a modeled 21 percent return keep the bull case credible, yet neither settles who bears depreciation when financing costs rise, and only 6 percent of the AI paper issued is investment grade. So the credit stack, not the demand, is where the buildout breaks first: if the short-term premium persists and the queued $50 to 60 billion of issuance needs wider concessions to clear, lenders are repricing the risk before the machines stop earning. The hardware is holding its price: rents on six-year-old A100s are up more than 20 percent this year, a direct read on willingness to pay that the backwardation signal does not capture (the case Oguz Erkan makes). Capacity is sold before it is built, so the borrowing is rational: $496 billion of backlog at AWS, $678 billion at Microsoft and $514 billion at Google Cloud (the case Market Sentiment makes). Open and Chinese models deliver comparable results at a fraction of the cost, so data-center pricing faces the race to the bottom that fiber ran after 1999 (the case Vitaliy Katsenelson makes).

docs.title: Does AI capex earn its return?
docs.text: Is the capex spending defense, or is the return not there? AI Spending Has Met Its First Real Bill Prove the return Capital intensity is not a moat. Every new AI dollar now has to out-earn its financing cost. Hyperscaler capital budgets are still climbing, about $800 billion a year across the four, $165 billion in the latest quarter, and spending has crossed operating cash flow: Alphabet's second-quarter free cash flow was negative $6 billion, its first negative quarter since the 2004 IPO. Once capex exceeds internal cash, the buildout needs outside money, and creditors now demand a premium on hyperscaler paper. That is the mechanism that turns scale from a moat into a test: the market rewards cash-backed returns and charges for faith, so every new AI dollar has to out-earn its financing cost. The bullish case regains force only if Alphabet's larger 2027 budget lifts the stock, cash generation catches up with investment and the two leading labs fund growth on durable, non-circular revenue. The spending is defense, so the return test is the wrong test: the risk of not investing is higher than the risk of overinvesting when a company's existence is at stake (the case Kris makes). The hyperscalers fund the buildout from profitable core businesses in advertising, cloud and software, unlike the dot-com suppliers, so affordability was never the question (the case Quanta 72 makes). The return is visible where the contracts are: Nebius, with multibillion-dollar deals with Microsoft and Meta, has a credible path to more than 4 GW of capacity by 2031 (the case Orbis Investments makes).

docs.title: Do frontier labs sell a commodity?
docs.text: What does a frontier lab sell: a commodity, or a premium? OpenAI and Anthropic Are Not the Same Business Split the trade Stop pricing OpenAI and Anthropic as one bet. One revenue line holds under pressure; the other has to be bought. Hyperscalers, lenders and investors have priced the two labs as one AI bet, and the revenue of the two behaves differently under pressure. OpenAI cut its API price by 80 percent as cheaper open and Chinese models took the routing, and lost $20.9 billion in 2025; Anthropic grew 142 percent quarter on quarter in the second quarter of 2026 against OpenAI's 18 percent, on enterprise coding that still monetizes, with $559 million of preliminary adjusted operating income for the June quarter. One revenue line holds when the token gets cheaper; the other has to be bought with price cuts. That is why the Call splits the trade rather than taking a side: what a lab sells depends on whether its margin survives the cluster's useful life, which only audited disclosure can show. Neither lab keeps a premium: Chinese open-weight models went from under 2 percent of token traffic in late 2024 to a majority of usage among the top models in 2026 (the case Massif Capital makes). The premium holds where the payoff is convex: commodity intelligence turns price-competitive in many applications, while finance and frontier research sustain premium pricing (the case Christian Catalini makes). Neither revenue line is what it seems: the labs pay their bills with venture funding of which Big Tech supplies roughly 40 percent, so the revenue Big Tech books from them is partly recycled (the case Ed Elson makes).

docs.title: Is power scarcity a moat?
docs.text: Is power scarcity a warning, or a moat? Power Doesn’t Depreciate. Its Premium Moves. Long access, not hardware This is a power-access trade before it is a chip trade. Own the permit and the interconnect, not the loudest fleet. Electricity is the constraint, but the premium belongs to whoever can turn a contracted megawatt into revenue on time. Compute can be ordered faster than power can be delivered: NVL72 deployment at full use needs about 23 gigawatts by 2027, while grids, substations and transformers take years to expand, and Nebius quotes $40 to 50 million for six months of capacity against $20 to 25 million for one to three years. A megawatt generates rent only when it arrives on schedule; a GPU parked behind a late interconnection generates cost. That is why the Call reads scarcity as a moat for the permit and the interconnect rather than for the hardware, and why it would change if the premium narrowed while power stayed scarce or a hyperscaler canceled because compute was sufficient. Permission is the asset politics can revoke: 70 to 75 percent of Americans oppose large data centers near their homes and more than half back a national moratorium (the case Michael Spencer makes). Scarcity is the warning fiber gave in 1999: capacity built on the expectation that demand keeps outrunning supply goes dark once a technical step multiplies what each unit can carry (the case Gaetano makes). The moat is financed, not owned: the builder's assets go obsolete faster than the buildings it leases, its largest customers are competing clouds and its only chip supplier is an investor (the case Kakashii makes).

docs.title: Why did the long end climb?
docs.text: Why did the long end climb after the hike: growth, debt, or a missing buyer? The Fed Hiked. The Long End Still Climbed. Supply sets the long end The bond market is pricing the AI bill, not a recession. The Fed cannot hike its way to a lower 10-year. The Fed raised short rates on September 16 and the 10-year Treasury still yielded 5.18 percent six trading days later, because the long end is priced by supply rather than by the policy rate. The federal deficit ran $1.97 trillion through August 2026 and the hyperscaler backlog stands near $2.3 trillion, so extraordinary capital spending and federal borrowing lean on the same bond market, while the Fed's short rate reaches only the households and borrowers it touches directly. Growth explains why the move is orderly; it does not make the refinancing bill disappear, and CleanSpark's 8.25 percent coupon shows today's rates reaching AI's borrowers. The Call would change if long yields fell while growth, inflation and AI capital spending stayed firm, or if Japanese and other foreign buyers returned in size without a better hedge. No buyer has gone missing: US term premia are broadly stable and recently lower, with no sign of rising against foreign equivalents, so the loss-of-confidence reading fails (the case Michael Howell makes). The long end is pricing inflation, not the AI bill: inflation stopped decelerating in 2023, and supercore PCE now rises about two points faster than before the pandemic (the case Matthew C. Klein makes). Yields are catching up with growth: with third-quarter GDP growth estimated at 5.1 percent plus inflation, a higher rate is no problem for an economy and for profits that grow faster than it (the case Kris makes). It is the debt, not the buyer: a hike feeds an annual interest bill approaching $1 trillion and a cut at 3.4 percent inflation loses the long end too, so the Fed is trapped either way (the case TSCS makes).

docs.title: Who funds the buildout?
docs.text: Who writes the checks for the buildout? AI Lenders Are Financing the End of Scarcity Lenders are mispricing scarcity Lenders are right to finance capacity and wrong to assume it stays scarce. Scarcity is a season; debt is a contract. Lenders are financing the capacity that will end the shortage they lend against. The spending has raced ahead of demonstrated revenue: the cash-flow forecasts behind the hyperscaler credit story need operating cash flow to roughly triple, from about $600 billion to $2 trillion, while off-balance-sheet commitments across five hyperscalers sit near $2.7 trillion and Oracle's free cash flow runs at negative $28.7 billion. Scarcity supports the collateral today, but every dollar lent adds the supply that erodes it, so a shortage of power, chips and capacity is a poor long-lived security against a fixed contract. The Call would change if September-quarter cash flow moved visibly toward $2 trillion, customer concentration fell sharply and the first Blackwell renewal held its price without new guarantees. The checks are already written by customers: AWS has had more demand than it can serve despite large Nvidia orders and its own Trainium chips, the best kind of spending there is (the case Kris makes). The spending pays for itself: next year's $1.2 trillion or more of AI capex should drive about $2 trillion of incremental revenue, a fraction of what AI generates as a business (the case Market Sentiment makes). Capex is durable, not fragile: the largest spenders keep reaffirming it while their margins still rise, and the customer base is broadening beyond the hyperscalers (the case Aurelion Research makes).

docs.title: Can agents break the habit?
docs.text: How fast do habits break? Habit Was the Moat. Agents Are Draining It. Sell habit, buy the rails Agents will drain weak consumer habits first. Back the rails (trust, records, distribution, compute), not the forgotten subscription. Meta's Muse has inserted itself between shoppers and sellers, and its economic position is what changes the bill. Muse is not merely answering; it chooses, pays and decides which seller is seen. A business paid by customer inertia, a forgotten subscription, a commodity brand, an ad-funded marketplace, loses the moment an agent makes comparison free, while trust, regulation, system-of-record status, distribution and compute remain defensible because the agent needs them to act. Paid consumer AI adoption is still about 3 percent, so the stock moves of September, Meta up 18 percent and AMD up 33 percent, are an early invoice rather than a finished income statement. The Call therefore backs the rails over the habit, and would change if Meta reported downloads without retained users, transaction volume or fees. The habit is not breaking yet: AI has produced many more apps and few successful ones, and paid consumer adoption sits near 3 percent, growing but still small (the case Moses Sternstein makes). The agent is not good enough to be chosen: a week of using Muse turned up quality and accuracy problems and no reason to prefer it over ChatGPT, and others will feel the same (the case Tae Kim makes). The dramatic prediction is usually wrong: radiology was to be taken over by AI within five years and instead more radiologists are needed, so the incumbents keep more than the Call allows (the case Jensen Huang makes).

docs.title: Does AI hardware hold its value?
docs.text: Does the hardware hold its value? The Bubble Is in the Denominator Cheap is conditional The market is not cheap. It is capitalizing AI earnings before anyone knows who owns them. The S&P 500 trades at 19.0 times forward earnings, and the market looks cheaper because profits surged. Those profits depend on AI spending: capital spending becomes supplier revenue and reported profit, so the denominator of the multiple is partly the buildout itself, while about $250 billion of hyperscaler bonds issued through August compete for the savings that set the discount rate, with the 10-year Treasury at 5.31 percent on October 5. Whether the profits are real depends on whether the hardware holds its value: if used-chip prices fall once scarcity fades and server lives prove shorter than the schedules, depreciation grows faster than operating income and the earnings being capitalized belong to no one yet. The Call would change if chip values held, productivity turned higher and lab revenue compounded. The hardware earns because it is used: GPUs are already running hot while the data says adoption and utilization are still early, so the capacity is not idle collateral (the case David George makes). Old chips still rent at a price: contracted lease rates and second-hand prices have held for chips launched three to six years ago, and compute is about 60 percent of hyperscaler capex (the case JunkBondInvestor makes). The checks are arriving: OpenAI's recurring revenue is nearing $70 billion, with enterprise sales more than doubled since July, so the earnings being capitalized have an owner (the case Tae Kim makes). The rise is earnings, not multiples: tech's forward multiple is up about 14 percent since October 2022, against 250 percent in the run to March 2000, so this is not 1999 (the case Ren makes).

docs.title: Do orders become profit?
docs.text: Do the orders turn into profit? The Backlog Is Not the Quarter Revenue yes, margin not yet The orders will ship. The profit comes later, and a margin that lags the ramp will be reported as a demand miss. AI suppliers report record order books, and the near book will ship: prepaid, supply-constrained demand converts into revenue at the pace of capacity. Profit arrives later than revenue. Between the order and the margin sit ramps that absorb fixed costs ahead of volume, payment terms stretched to a year at Nvidia for its best-rated customers, revenue deferred until a deployment is complete, a far book outgrowing the near one three to one at Microsoft, 113 percent against 37 percent, and assets whose life the buyers' own lenders now cover with guarantees, $28 billion at Meta. So the Call reads the near book as revenue, the far book as a promise and the margin as the number that arrives last, and expects a margin that lags the ramp to be reported as a demand miss. The margin is not the number to watch: what matters is earnings growth against the capital required to produce it, and Meta in 2023 shows the cash-flow math working once the ramp passes (the case Gaetano makes). Supply, not demand, binds the quarter: Nvidia's unconstrained growth could run above 100 percent against guidance near 70 percent, so a shortfall is a supply story (the case Aurelion Research makes). The far book is less than a promise: Amazon's backlog went from $200 billion at a 3.8-year average life to $496 billion at 6.4 years in nine months, a stretching, not a filling (the case Michael Burry makes).

docs.title: Does the frontier model still command a price?
docs.text: Does the frontier model still command a price? The Model Is Not the Price The price has left the model A frontier model no longer commands a price per token for long. The lab still does, and only a prospectus says what that price is worth. The token is cheap and getting cheaper. The gap between the Chinese open models and the frontier is about four months by Torsten Slok's reading of Epoch, a majority of tokens on the platforms that count them had moved to open or Chinese models by September, and Anthropic's Opus 5.5 lists at $4 per million input tokens against OpenAI's $10, a 60 percent undercut. What still commands a price is the lab: the completed job, the distribution, the dollars that have not yet followed the volume. But no audited figure for that price is on EDGAR; $50 billion, $65 billion and $70 billion are three run-rate readings on three dates, and only a registration statement puts them on one line. The Call expects the filing to show a lab that is paid, in part by its investors. The labs' price shows in the capex they pull: $1.2 trillion or more of AI capex next year should drive about $2 trillion of incremental revenue, with no prospectus needed (the case Market Sentiment makes). The frontier is still paid, and paid more each year: Anthropic's run-rate went from $1 billion at the end of 2024 to $9 billion a year later and almost $50 billion by May 2026 (the case Longriver makes). No one commands a price, the lab included: OpenAI's price cut with a tenfold jump in usage looks like the start of a price war between Anthropic, OpenAI and the Chinese models (the case Steve Eisman makes). One lab commands the price and the other does not: Anthropic is far ahead of OpenAI in model quality and ARR before its IPO, and the lead should widen with the proceeds (the case Michael Spencer makes).

docs.title: Who pays for the AI power bill?
docs.text: Who pays for the AI power bill? The Ratepayer Pays First The ratepayer pays first Data centers pay for their own wires. The higher capacity price their demand sets lands first on every PJM household's bill. Data centers pay for what they cause at their own sites: Google funds its lines and upgrades, Texas asks large loads for $50,000 of security per megawatt, and a data center pays the capacity price on its own load. What none of them pays is the rise its demand causes in the price every other customer pays, and PJM's market monitor told FERC on December 5, 2025, that no state tariff can shield retail customers from it. Households in PJM's nine jurisdictions paid a median 11.7 percent more per kilowatt-hour over the year to July, against 5.6 percent elsewhere. Retail prices also move with fuel and with rate cases, so the gap is consistent with the transfer without proving it; the federal price data and the December auction are the test. The capacity price answers a forecast, not a delivered load: large loads add volatility to the forecast because timelines move with construction, permitting and owner decisions (the case NERC makes). Cost causation shields the household: assign every cost to the load that causes it, as Google asks ERCOT and the Commission to do, and the data center pays for its own lines and upgrades (the case Google makes). Bring-your-own power removes the transfer: co-located generation, structured correctly, improves reliability, lowers ratepayer costs and speeds the buildout at once (the case Crusoe Energy makes). The demand setting the price is partly phantom: ERCOT assessed more than 410 GW of large-load requests, 87 percent from data centers, against a Texas peak near 85 GW (the case Reyk Knuhtsen makes).

docs.title: Is AI revenue arriving fast enough for the biggest spenders to pay for their data centers out of their own cash?
docs.text: Is AI revenue arriving fast enough for the biggest spenders to pay for their data centers out of their own cash? The Cash Arrives Unevenly Only Microsoft pays with room to spare Microsoft pays for its build from its own cash. Alphabet and Meta spend most of theirs; Amazon spends more than its operations bring in.

docs.title: remaining performance obligations
docs.text: RPO Contracted revenue a company has not yet recognized; the filing's name for backlog. Remaining performance obligations are the revenue a company is contracted to deliver but has not yet recognized. Filings split them into the part due within twelve months and the part due later; the split is the near book and the far book of Part 11.

docs.title: Treasury International Capital
docs.text: TIC The Treasury's monthly report of foreign holdings of U.S. securities, including each country's Treasuries. The Treasury International Capital system reports, with a lag of about six weeks, how much of U.S. securities foreign holders own, country by country. Its table of major foreign holders settles the question of whether Japan bought or sold Treasuries in a given month (test p07-t02).

docs.title: forward multiple
docs.text: forward P/E forward earnings forward price-to-earnings times forward earnings The share price divided by the next twelve months' expected earnings per share. The forward multiple divides today's price by the earnings analysts expect over the next twelve months. It is a valuation, not a forecast: a lower multiple can mean a cheaper market or earnings expectations that have run ahead of what will be delivered, which is the denominator question of Part 10.

docs.title: residual-value guarantee
docs.text: residual value guarantee residual-value guarantees A promise to make up the difference if an asset is worth less than expected at the end of a lease. A residual-value guarantee is a commitment to cover the gap if a leased or partnered asset is worth less at the end of the term than the contract assumed. Meta's $28 billion guarantee on its data-center venture (Part 11) is a liability that lives outside the balance sheet until the asset's value is tested.

docs.title: token
docs.text: tokens per million tokens price per million tokens The unit a language model is priced by: a fragment of text, roughly three quarters of a word. A token is the unit a language model reads and writes, about three quarters of an English word. Model prices are quoted per million tokens, input and output priced separately. When the price per token falls while usage rises, the question is whether the lab is paid for the token or for something else: Part 12.

docs.title: option-adjusted spread
docs.text: OAS A bond index's spread over Treasuries after adjusting for the options embedded in the bonds. The option-adjusted spread is the spread of a bond or index over the Treasury curve after removing the value of embedded options such as early redemption. ICE BofA publishes it daily for its indices, and FRED carries the series, which is why the Docket uses it to settle questions about investment-grade credit.

docs.title: days sales outstanding
docs.text: DSO How many days of sales sit unpaid in receivables; longer terms raise it. Days sales outstanding measures how long customers take to pay: receivables divided by daily sales. When a supplier stretches terms from 90 days to a year, as Nvidia did for its best-rated customers (Part 11), the number rises and the quarter's revenue arrives in cash much later.

docs.title: depreciation
docs.text: useful life useful lives depreciation schedule The accounting charge that spreads an asset's cost over the years it is assumed to last. Depreciation spreads the cost of a long-lived asset over its assumed useful life. The assumption is a choice: a server depreciated over six years looks more profitable each year than the same server over three. When chips go obsolete faster than the schedule says, reported profits flatter the economics; that is the argument of Parts 03, 05 and 10.

docs.title: capacity auction
docs.text: Base Residual Auction capacity price capacity auctions The auction in which a grid operator buys commitments to be available in a future year; its clearing price lands on every bill. In a capacity auction a grid operator such as PJM buys commitments from power plants to be available in a delivery year three years out. The clearing price, set by the last unit needed, is paid on every customer's load. A price cap limits it; whether the December 9, 2026 auction clears below the cap is a test on the Docket.

docs.title: capital spending
docs.text: capex capital expenditure capital expenditures Cash a company spends on long-lived assets: data centers, chips, networks, power. Capital spending, or capex, is the cash a company puts into assets that last years: land, buildings, servers, chips, grid connections. It leaves the cash-flow statement at once and reaches the income statement slowly, through depreciation. The AI buildout is measured in capex because that is where the money moves first.

docs.title: new-issue concession
docs.text: concession concessions The extra yield a borrower offers on a new bond, above where its existing bonds trade, to get the deal done. A new-issue concession is the extra yield a borrower pays on a new bond relative to its outstanding bonds, so that buyers absorb the supply. Widening concessions mean lenders are charging more scrutiny; DeepStack reads them as evidence, and settles tests on public spread series instead.

docs.title: credit default swap
docs.text: CDS Insurance on a borrower's debt, priced in basis points a year; a higher price means a riskier borrower. A credit default swap pays the buyer if a borrower defaults. Its price, in basis points a year, is the market's running estimate of that risk: Oracle's five-year CDS at a record 227 basis points (Part 08) said lenders had started to charge for the buildout.

docs.title: PJM
docs.text: PJM Interconnection The grid operator for thirteen states and the District of Columbia, from New Jersey to Illinois. PJM Interconnection runs the wholesale electricity market and the transmission grid for about 65 million people across thirteen states and the District of Columbia. Its capacity auctions set the price every household in the region pays for reliability, which is the mechanism of Part 13.

docs.title: real yield
docs.text: TIPS inflation-protected real yields The yield on a Treasury whose principal rises with inflation: the price of money after inflation. A real yield is the yield on Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities, whose principal follows the consumer price index. It is the cost of borrowing after inflation, the number a lender financing a data center locks in. The nominal 10-year yield minus the real yield is the breakeven inflation the bond market prices.

docs.title: the Call’s number
docs.text: Call’s number callProbability The chance, from 0 to 100, that the Call gives the yes answer to a test’s question, recorded before the test’s date. Every pre-specified test on the Docket can carry the Call’s number: the chance the house gives the yes answer to the test’s question, written into the record with the words of the test and before its date, so it cannot be set in hindsight. It prints on the Docket, in the Part’s list of tests, on the home strip and on the Result, on one line from 0 (no) to 100 (yes), with the readers’ share beside it once 25 have clicked. It is DeepStack’s reading, not a market price and not advice; from the tenth result it feeds the Brier score.

docs.title: interconnection
docs.text: grid connection interconnections The physical and contractual link that lets a site draw power from the grid; the queue to get one can take years. Interconnection is the connection of a load or a generator to the transmission grid, with the studies, upgrades and approvals it requires. A contracted megawatt is not a connected megawatt until the interconnection is energized, which is why Parts 06 and 13 separate the two.

docs.title: free cash flow
docs.text: free cash flows Operating cash flow minus capital spending: the cash left after the company has paid for its own buildout. Free cash flow is the cash from operations minus capital spending. A company with strong profits and negative free cash flow is funding its buildout from outside: debt, leases, partners or investors. Alphabet's first negative quarter since its IPO (Part 04) is the example DeepStack keeps coming back to.

docs.title: earnings yield
docs.text: earnings yields Expected earnings divided by price: the inverse of the forward multiple, comparable in shape to a bond yield. The earnings yield is expected earnings divided by price, the forward multiple turned upside down. At 19 times forward earnings the yield is about 5.3%. It is compared with the 10-year Treasury as a valuation sensitivity, not as a like-for-like return: earnings are not contractual, and the two assets differ in duration, growth and risk.

docs.title: private credit
docs.text: Loans made by funds rather than banks or public bond markets, usually to one borrower at a time. Private credit is lending by investment funds outside banks and public bond markets, often secured on specific assets such as chips or data centers. It financed the compute platforms of Part 01 and the facilities of Part 03; its terms are rarely public, which is why DeepStack reads them from filings and dated reports.

docs.title: spread
docs.text: credit spread spreads The extra yield a borrower pays above a Treasury of the same maturity, in basis points. A credit spread is the yield on a bond minus the yield on a Treasury of the same maturity. It is the market's price for the risk that the borrower does not pay. Spreads are quoted in basis points; a wider spread means dearer credit. DeepStack reads spreads on FRED series and in filings, never from a dealer's note.

docs.title: EIA-861M
docs.text: Form EIA-861M The federal monthly survey of electricity sales and revenue by state and customer class. Form EIA-861M is the U.S. Energy Information Administration's monthly survey of electricity sales, revenue and customers by state and customer class. Revenue divided by sales gives the average price per kilowatt-hour; DeepStack computes the household price from it, as first published, for the tests of Part 13.

docs.title: Call informed
docs.text: A result on a test where the Call expected either answer: the result informs the Call and is not scored. When a specification records that either answer fits the Call, the result is read as Call informed: it changes what the Call knows without counting as held or missed. The Call’s number on such a test still prints and still enters the Brier score.

docs.title: hyperscaler
docs.text: hyperscalers One of the largest cloud and platform companies that build data centers at continental scale. A hyperscaler is one of the handful of companies, Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta and Oracle among them, that build and run data centers at a scale measured in gigawatts and tens of billions of dollars a quarter. Their capital budgets, backlogs and cash flows are the largest single inputs to the AI economy.

docs.title: open weights
docs.text: open-weight open-weights open weight A model whose trained parameters are published, so anyone can run it without paying the lab. An open-weight model publishes its trained parameters. Anyone can download and run it, which puts a ceiling on what a closed model can charge for comparable capability. The gap in months between the best open model and the frontier is one of the numbers DeepStack tracks.

docs.title: basis point
docs.text: basis points bp bps One hundredth of a percentage point: 25 basis points is 0.25%. A basis point is one hundredth of one percent. Yields and spreads move in basis points because the differences that matter are small: a 10-year Treasury moving from 5.00% to 5.31% has risen 31 basis points.

docs.title: term premium
docs.text: term premia The extra yield investors demand to hold a long bond instead of rolling short ones. The term premium is the part of a long-dated yield that compensates for holding duration rather than rolling short bills. When the Fed raises short rates and long yields rise more, the market is charging for time: supply, deficits and a thinner buyer base, as Part 07 argues.

docs.title: large load
docs.text: large loads large-load A customer, typically a data center, whose demand is big enough to need its own grid rules. A large load is a single customer whose electricity demand is large enough that grid operators and regulators write rules for it: deposits, batch studies, requirements to bring its own capacity. Data centers are the large loads of this cycle.

docs.title: Brier score
docs.text: Brier The mean of the squared gap between the chance the Call gave the yes answer and what happened; 0 is perfect and 0.25 is what a coin flip earns. DeepStack prints the Brier score on the Scorecard from the tenth result whose test carried a number recorded before the date. For each such result the gap is the Call’s number as a fraction minus one when the answer was yes, or minus zero when it was no, squared; the score is the mean of the gaps. A Call that said 85% and was right adds 0.02; one that said 15% and was wrong adds 0.72. Lower is better, 0.25 is what a coin flip earns, and the score punishes confidence the source did not reward.

docs.title: Call missed
docs.text: A result that came in against what the Call expected. The reading against the Call when the answer is the one the Call did not expect. It sits beside the test’s own answer (yes or no) and counts in the hit rate from the tenth result.

docs.title: backlog
docs.text: order book backlogs Orders a company has accepted but not yet delivered or recognized as revenue. A backlog is the stock of orders a company has accepted but not yet delivered. It is a promise of revenue, not revenue: it converts at the pace of capacity, and the part due within a year is worth more to the quarter than the part due later. Filings split the two, which is why DeepStack reads the near book and the far book separately.

docs.title: CCC
docs.text: CCC-rated CCC spread The lowest rating tier of bonds that still trade actively; the riskiest corner of the credit market. CCC is the rating tier just above default. The spread of CCC bonds over Treasuries, published daily on FRED, is the price of the riskiest credit; at 1,146 basis points on September 28 (Part 08) it measured how much lenders charged the weakest borrowers while financing the strongest.

docs.title: ratepayer
docs.text: ratepayers A customer who pays a regulated electricity bill; in the AI buildout, the household that pays first. A ratepayer is any customer billed under a regulated tariff. The word matters because a data center that pays for its own wires still raises the capacity price every other ratepayer pays, which is the argument of Part 13.

docs.title: split Call
docs.text: A Call whose tone is neither constructive nor skeptical: it takes a side on the question without a bullish or bearish lean on the trade. A split Call is one of the three tones a DeepStack Call can carry, with constructive and skeptical. The tone says how the Call leans on the trade; the side says what the Call holds on the question. A split Call still takes a side on the question (Part 13 holds that the ratepayer pays first) while staking no direction on the market. The Scorecard counts the tones of every Call.

docs.title: megawatt
docs.text: MW gigawatt GW megawatts gigawatts A unit of power: a megawatt serves a few hundred homes, a gigawatt a city; data centers are sized in both. A megawatt is a million watts of power; a gigawatt is a thousand megawatts. Data centers are sized by the power they draw because electricity is the binding constraint: a gigawatt campus needs its own substation, its own interconnection and, increasingly, its own generation.

docs.title: Call held
docs.text: A result that came in the way the Call expected, whatever the test’s question asked. Each pre-specified test records the answer the Call expected (yes, no, or either). When the test resolves, the result is read against that expectation: Call held when the answer is the one the Call expected, Call missed when it is the one the Call did not expect. The test’s own answer wears its own chip beside the reading, so a rule that says “yes if” and the seal never share a word. The hit rate counts Calls held among pre-specified tests, from the tenth result.

docs.title: duration
docs.text: How far in the future a payment or a return sits, and how sensitive its value is to interest rates. Duration measures how far out a stream of payments sits and therefore how much its present value moves when rates change. A fifteen-year data-center lease, a far backlog and a growth stock are all long-duration promises; a higher 10-year yield taxes each of them.

docs.title: re-let
docs.text: re-lets relet Renting out compute capacity again when a contract ends, at whatever the market then pays. A re-let is the second lease of the same capacity after the first contract ends. The re-let rate, as a share of the original price, says whether the hardware kept its value: near 95% supports durable economics, and a fast decay exposes the depreciation argument.

docs.title: Who is on each side: Is the marginal buyer of AI compute real?
docs.text: Nvidia’s Demand Is Real. Its Financing Is Fragile. Manufactured Michael Burry: Much and possibly most of current and future AI compute demand is not end-customer demand; the majority of future revenues are financed through a circular off-balance-sheet arrangement. Michael Burry: NVIDIA's revenue growth is only mostly real because circular financing sustains marginal AI compute demand above market-rate levels, and resolution of the power bottleneck will reduce revenue recurrence and compress the scarcity premium in margins… Strongest case against Manufactured: Invest in Assets: A visibility window that extends by a full year across the customer base is much harder to manufacture than a single-customer beat and signals that AI demand is structural rather than lumpy. Insatiable Kris: The Google SpaceX GPU rental is bullish for Nvidia because there are still not enough GPUs to quench demand; Nvidia ramps production continuously but cannot follow demand. Invest in Assets: A visibility window that extends by a full year across the customer base is much harder to manufacture than a single-customer beat and signals that AI demand is structural rather than lumpy. Strongest case against Insatiable: Michael Burry: Much and possibly most of current and future AI compute demand is not end-customer demand; the majority of future revenues are financed through a circular off-balance-sheet arrangement. Voices that cross sides Longriver: Long since 2025, and author of the bear case's most honest sentence. Kris: Bullish on demand, and endorses the GFC earnings-quality parallel. NZS Capital: Exited on the bear case; re-entered when the price paid for the risk.

docs.title: Who is on each side: SpaceX after the IPO: exit liquidity, or the next ten-bagger?
docs.text: SpaceX Is Funding an AI Bet Before the Proof Exit liquidity Kris: Retail buyers of the SpaceX IPO are the exit liquidity: the fancy name for paying insiders, VCs and early investors at peak hype valuations. Kris: The Google SpaceX GPU rental is bullish for Nvidia because there are still not enough GPUs to quench demand; Nvidia ramps production continuously but cannot follow demand. Kakashii: SpaceX deployed 0.4 gigawatts of nameplate compute in the last quarter while Musk promises more than 10 gigawatts by end-2027 and describes close to 15 gigawatts at the PowerPoint level. Kakashii: SpaceX's AI segment reveals the industry's bad accounting habits: how AI revenue is counted, what is hidden in construction-in-progress, and where the Nvidia GPUs everyone calls short-supplied actually are. Strongest case against Exit liquidity: Trey Henninger: SpaceX at roughly 100 times trailing revenue would never qualify as a value investment, yet it is feasibly a ten-bagger: an extreme bull scenario could carry the company toward an 18 trillion dollar valuation or beyond over ten to twenty-five years. The number is real Jeremie Eliahou Ontiveros: Selling frontier-model inference is extraordinarily profitable: on a GB300 cluster, OpenAI and Anthropic can generate over 100 billion dollars per gigawatt-year of revenue against roughly 12 billion of rental cost. Jeremie Eliahou Ontiveros: SpaceX is on track to build about 10 gigawatts of datacenter capacity by year-end 2027; independent site-by-site evaluation supports the guided 6 to 8 incremental gigawatts, implying a path to 300 billion dollars of ARR with only half the… Strongest case against The number is real: Michael Burry: NVIDIA's revenue growth is only mostly real because circular financing sustains marginal AI compute demand above market-rate levels, and resolution of the power bottleneck will reduce revenue recurrence and compress the scarcity premium in margins… Voices that cross sides Trey Henninger: SpaceX at roughly 100 times trailing revenue would never qualify as a value investment, yet it is feasibly a ten-bagger: an extreme bull scenario could carry the company toward an 18 trillion dollar valuation or beyond over ten to twenty-five years. JunkBondInvestor: Lenders back Starlink's cash and bet the AI spend never drains the company. Kevin Gee: Long AI in the long run, doubtful the market absorbs three $1T cash-burning IPOs at once.

docs.title: Who is on each side: The debt behind the machines: 1999 capex, 2008 credit, or neither?
docs.text: The Machines Will Work. docs.title: Steve Eisman (Steven Eisman)

Steve Eisman, in The Real Eisman Playbook, relays the case that the industry is only in year three of an eight-to-ten-year buildout, comparable to building the Las Vegas Strip in the 1950s. Steve Eisman writes that investors rewarded whoever spent the most for two years, then started asking who would earn a return. Steve Eisman reported the same gap a fortnight later, with a brutal addendum: OpenAI’s costs rose about $3bn against roughly $1bn of new revenue. Steve Eisman, in a conversation with Ed Zitron, draws the darker inference: data centers are harder and costlier to build than planned, gigawatt projects are late, and every month of slippage gives customers who already lose money more time to stumble. Treasury buybacks of long bonds, $4 billion and then $6 billion, held yields down for one day, Steve Eisman points out. George Noble, speaking with Steve Eisman, starts from roughly $40 trillion of federal debt and concludes that no Treasury secretary can talk rates down against that weight. Steve Eisman estimates that about 70% of the AI revenue hyperscalers book comes directly or indirectly from those two labs. A rate hike and an oil shock moved markets in the same weeks, and Steve Eisman argues that nothing but oil and interest rates matters right now. Against that growth sits the loss-making base of the chain: Steve Eisman, in an episode with Ed Zitron, cited OpenAI’s $20.9 billion loss in 2025 on $13.07 billion of revenue. Steve Eisman calls 5% the Rubicon, while noting that oil and the 10-year are the two variables that matter and neither is predictable. George Noble, on Steve Eisman's program on September 21, reads the same demand from the other end: a vendor funding its customers' purchases is not evidence that the money underneath is solid. Steve Eisman, on September 11, read OpenAI's cut on its GPT model, with a reported tenfold jump in usage, as the beginning of a price war in AI services; by September 28 he called a price war among the two labs and the Chinese models the chief risk to the AI story. Voices that cross sides: If AI becomes cheaper and commoditized, spending hundreds of billions of dollars becomes much harder to justify economically. Voices that cross sides: The bullish case compares current AI infrastructure buildout to building the Las Vegas Strip in the 1950s, arguing that enormous upfront investment creates an eventually valuable economic ecosystem. Scarcity as a warning: Data centers are proving more difficult and costly to build than expected, with gigawatt-scale projects running behind schedule, and every delay gives an already-unprofitable customer base more time to encounter financial strain. Debt: 99% of GDP, up from 35%: Treasury Secretary Bessent's $4 billion to $6 billion effort to buy long Treasuries and push rates down failed, as rates went up anyway, and his speaking at a partisan political convention undermined his credibility with the bond market. Debt: 99% of GDP, up from 35%: Ten-year Treasury yields have broken through 4.8% and then 4.9%, the highest level since November 2023, driven by the Iran war pushing oil prices above $100. Guarantees, not faith: George Noble's bear case for AI rests on the question of actual return on investment; he argues that Nvidia announcing massive funding packages just to keep customers like OpenAI able to keep buying chips shows the money underneath the boom is not… Guarantees, not faith: George Noble cites an estimate from Julien Garran at MacroStrategy putting AI malinvestment at roughly twenty four times what was seen during the dot com bubble. Not the customers, yet: Nvidia's top five customers accounted for seventy percent of accounts receivable for the quarter, and some of those customers including OpenAI are not in especially healthy financial condition. Not the customers, yet: Bessent's announced program to buy $4 billion, later raised to $6 billion, in long term Treasuries worked for one day before rates marched higher, so he needs a much bigger bazooka or an alternative buyer. A backlog is a promise: There is a chain where NVIDIA sells chips to hyperscalers, hyperscalers' capital spending depends on the future health of OpenAI and Anthropic, and both are currently losing substantial sums, with OpenAI's revenue growth having slowed relative to… Shipping is not earning: Nvidia's top five customers accounted for seventy percent of accounts receivable for the quarter, and some of those customers including OpenAI are not in especially healthy financial condition. Voices that cross sides: Off-balance-sheet AI financing is back because costs are exploding: Nvidia raised prices 15%, data centers are expensive and slow to build, and the big cloud companies that used to be capital-light cash machines will spend something like $700… Open weights set the price: OpenAI's price cut on its GPT model, combined with a reported tenfold jump in usage, looks like the beginning of a price war in AI services. Open weights set the price: Steve says the AI story probably continues as long as token growth keeps rising, and identifies a price war between Anthropic, OpenAI and the Chinese models as the main risk that could change it. The filing sets the price: Anthropic looks likely to file for an IPO soon, and it will want to do that while token usage numbers are still near their peak, before the picture gets less flattering.
